title: Thermal and Structural Properties of Locally Available Drum-Kiln Insulation Materials for Biochar Production in Zambia: A Literature-Based Synthesis
content: Drum kilns lose a substantial fraction of their fuel energy through the wall, and in Zambia the materials best suited to reducing this loss are locally abundant and inexpensive. This paper presents a consolidated, literature-based assessment of the insulation materials available to a rural fabricator, comprising anthill (termite-mound) clay, clay–sand and cement–sand mixtures, fired clay brick, and, as a reference case, commercial ceramic fibre. The study is a structured cross-literature synthesis rather than a new experimental characterisation, and no specimens were tested. Measured data were assembled from the peer-reviewed literature through a documented search, the measurement method, test temperature, and specimen condition behind each value were recorded, and, because no validated conversion between methods exists, the values were reported as method-stratified ranges rather than numerically normalised across the guarded-hot-plate, transient plane-source, and laser-flash methods. The resulting trends in thermal conductivity, strength, and porosity were analysed against agro-waste content and firing temperature. Published analyses of anthill clay from Ghana, Nigeria, and Kenya, used here as analogues because no Zambian analysis was found, indicate a kaolinitic refractory raw material containing approximately 52 to 63 percent silica and 16 to 31 percent alumina; local XRF and XRD testing is therefore a prerequisite for design specification. Reported composites containing 10 to 15 weight percent sawdust exhibit room-temperature thermal conductivities of 0.26 to 0.32 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹, comparable to fired insulating brick and roughly one fifth or less of the value for dense cement–sand mortar, while retaining cold crushing strengths of approximately 6 to 9 MPa, above a 5 MPa screening criterion adopted here for a self-supporting lining, provided the agro-waste fraction does not exceed approximately 15 weight percent. Ceramic fibre offers the lowest conductivity, near 0.07 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹, but its fragility and cost render it unsuitable for the target context. None of the locally available materials simultaneously offers the lowest conductivity, adequate strength, and durability under thermal cycling; a layered wall, in which an anthill-clay composite performs the principal insulating function behind a thin protective face, is therefore proposed as a preliminary design implication that has yet to be tested experimentally or numerically. The compiled ranges, stratified by measurement method and traceable to their sources in a supplementary dataset, are intended as bounded inputs for subsequent modelling and for the local testing that must precede design.
